# Edge and On-Device Deployment {#sec-edge}

Most of this book serves models from a datacenter. The other end of the wire is
the device in a pocket. This chapter covers running models on phones, laptops,
and the neural accelerators inside them: why you would, what the constraints are,
and the models and runtimes built for the regime. By the end a reader can explain
why on-device models are small by design rather than shrunk after the fact, why
quantization is pushed harder at the edge than in the cloud, and what the
cloud-versus-edge split actually optimizes.

## Why run on the edge

Four pulls move inference onto the device. Privacy: the data never leaves the
phone, which is decisive for messages, photos, and health. Latency: no network
round-trip, so a response can start immediately. Availability: it works on a
plane or in a dead zone. And cost: there is no per-token serving bill to anyone.
Against all four stands one hard wall. A phone has orders of magnitude less
memory, compute, and power than a datacenter accelerator, no high-bandwidth
memory, and a thermal budget measured in single-digit watts. That wall shapes
every choice below.

## Small by design, not shrunk

You cannot take a 70-billion-parameter model and shrink it onto a phone; the
on-device tier is architected for the regime from the start. MobileLLM finds that
below a billion parameters the usual data-and-scale story yields to architecture:
deep-and-thin networks beat wide-and-shallow ones at the same size, and embedding
sharing with grouped-query attention closes much of the gap to far larger models
on tasks like API calling [@liu2024mobilellm]. OpenELM allocates parameters
non-uniformly across layers, a layer-wise scaling that squeezes more accuracy
from a fixed budget, and ships with conversion to Apple's MLX for on-device
inference [@mehta2024openelm].

The vendors ship this as a tier. Gemini Nano is the on-device size, 1.8 and 3.25
billion parameters, distilled from larger Gemini models and 4-bit quantized for
deployment [@gemini2023]. Apple's on-device foundation model is about three
billion parameters trained with 2-bit quantization-aware training and KV-cache
sharing, with small LoRA adapters swapped in per feature, while a larger model
waits in Private Cloud Compute for the hard requests [@apple2025foundation]. The
shared pattern is a small local model for the common case and an escape hatch to
the cloud for the rest.

## Quantization to the bone

Server quantization (@sec-quantization-kernels) trades a little quality for
throughput; on the edge, memory is the budget, so the pressure is harder. BitNet
b1.58 takes it to the limit with ternary weights drawn from {-1, 0, 1}, about
1.58 bits each, reported to match a full-precision transformer of the same size
and training tokens in perplexity from roughly three billion parameters upward
while cutting memory and energy sharply, the regime where the matrix multiply
collapses toward addition [@ma2024bitnet]. Whether one-bit-class training holds
at frontier scale is unsettled, but the memory and energy case for the edge is
direct: the device's budget is counted in bits per weight.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
params = 3e9                        # a 3B on-device model
phone_budget_gb = 4.0              # memory you can spend on weights
for bits in [16, 8, 4, 2, 1.58]:
    gb = params * bits / 8 / 1e9
    fits = "fits" if gb <= phone_budget_gb else "too big"
    print(f"{bits:>4} bits/weight -> {gb:4.1f} GB weights  ({fits})")
print("memory is the budget: quantization is what makes a model fit on the edge")
```
::::

## The runtime

The pragmatic substrate is software like llama.cpp, a dependency-light C/C++
inference engine that runs on plain CPUs and on Apple silicon through Metal and
NEON, with the single-file GGUF format carrying the quantized weights and their
metadata [@llamacpp]. The dedicated accelerators, Apple's Neural Engine,
Qualcomm's Hexagon, and mobile GPUs, are faster per watt, but each has its own
runtime, operator support, and quantization formats, so the edge is fragmented in
a way the CUDA-centric datacenter is not. A portable GGUF model on the CPU is
often the floor you can rely on everywhere, with an NPU path added where the
hardware and toolchain allow.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
How much inference ends up on the device is unsettled. One view holds that
on-device models will absorb most everyday requests as phone memory grows and
small-model quality climbs, leaving the cloud for the genuinely hard tasks. The
other holds that the capability gap to frontier models is large and widening
faster than device budgets grow, so the edge stays a privacy-and-offline niche
while real work goes to the cloud. Both pulls are real, and the split a product
draws depends on whether its hardest request, not its median one, has to run
locally.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The device's memory budget reaches all the way back into pretraining. A model
that does not fit in a phone's memory at a usable token rate cannot be served
there at all, so the on-device tier is trained small and quantization-aware from
the start rather than pruned afterward, and Apple's 2-bit quantization-aware
training is exactly this constraint made into a training objective. The
hardware's memory dictates not just the model's size but how it is trained, the
sharpest version of the constraint arrow that runs through the book.
:::
